# docs_audit_report — 2026-08-22

## TL;DR (stranger's 30-second take)
I would close the tab. The opening explains Carnot reasonably well, but the contradictory license, wall of unexplained metrics, and conspicuously perfect results make the page feel like an internal research dashboard trying too hard to establish credibility.

## TOP 3 PROBLEMS
1. The license contradicts itself — “MIT-0” in the hero and metadata vs “Apache 2.0 License” in the footer.
2. “What we measured” is a 12-card jargon wall — FoVer, CRANE, VeriCoT, HalluGuard, CCTU, PRM-BiasBench, and other unexplained names bury the evidence.
3. “Recent progress,” “Research operations,” and “Preprint” read like internal status reports — paper-v6, repinning, operator-initiated upload, autonomous agents, retractions, and audit plumbing.

## DETAILED FINDINGS
### Bloat
- Navigation — 12 text links plus 2 platform buttons — cap at roughly 5–7 primary choices.
- Hero statistics — 5 items, including a prose-heavy “Recent progress” card — cap at 3 user-relevant outcomes; experiment, milestone, and test counts are vanity metrics.
- Evidence — 12 unrelated result cards — cap at 4–6 primary, comparable results and move the rest to the report.
- How it works + Capabilities + Evidence + Writing — 30 cards collectively — no single section exceeds 20, but the page still becomes a card wall.
- Writing — 7 blog cards, mostly about internal failures and operations — cap at 3 selected articles.
- Longest bento body — “Why ‘Energy-Based’?” at approximately 72 words — below the 120-word hard limit.
- Longest result-card body — “Recent progress” at approximately 47 words — below the 60-word hard limit.
- Footer paragraph — 8 words — below the 100-word hard limit.
- HTML structure — repeated stray closing `div` elements and a premature grid close leave “Test-Time Compute (TTC) & PREM” outside the capabilities grid — repair the structure before judging the intended visual density.

### Internal jargon
- Hero statistics and “Recent progress” — `AUROC`, `FoVer`, `5-seed dual-condition`, `architecture-only`, `v2`, and “repinned” — this sounds like experiment bookkeeping, not evidence a newcomer can interpret.
- “Why Energy-Based?” — `gradient`, `FPGA Ising machines`, and `thermodynamic samplers` — none is translated into a practical user benefit or supported performance claim.
- “Typed constraints” — `CCTU constrained tool-use micro-benchmark` — an unexplained benchmark name paired with tiny percentages.
- “Multi-step reasoning” — `AND-composed` — implementation shorthand that obscures what passing all checks means.
- “Research operations” — `autonomous research loop`, `inner agent`, `adversarial-verify pass`, and `structured JSON record` — internal process vocabulary presented as a customer capability.
- “APIs & portable memory” — `MCP`, `VerdictRecord`, and `SessionMemory` — product-internal type names and an unexplained acronym.
- “Test-Time Compute (TTC) & PREM” — two acronyms in the title, followed by “Process-Reward Energy Model variance” and “intrinsic motivation” — nearly meaningless without research context.
- Evidence cards — `KV260 FPGA`, `HumanEval-50`, `EstimationVerifier`, `SVAMP`, `FoVer`, `CRANE`, `VeriCoT`, `GSM8K`, `TP rate`, `PRM-BiasBench`, `k=5`, `HalluGuard v3`, `pp`, and `CCTU` — the section requires a glossary before it can be evaluated.
- Preprint — `paper-v6`, `checked-in experiment artifacts`, `continuous-integration checkout`, `non-operator environment`, and `operator-initiated upload` — repository and workflow language leaking into public copy.
- No raw `Exp 1688`, `.148`-style milestone IDs, `X/Y criteria met`, or `foo=True` flags appear. The page nevertheless contains the same class of insider-facing language.

### Per-milestone narrative
- Hero statistics — “5,725 Experiment runs” and “382 Completed milestones” report internal throughput rather than user value.
- “Recent progress” — “Repinned from v2 0.9857 after pre-submission adversarial audit” reads like a changelog entry.
- “Research operations” — the planner/inner-agent/adversarial-verification description is an internal development retrospective masquerading as a capability.
- Preprint — “paper-v6” and “arXiv submission is prepared but pending operator-initiated upload” are status-board notes.
- Writing — retractions, fatal findings, detector rules, audit rounds, dogfooding counts, and “what we shipped” dominate the public narrative.
- No literal “Milestone .120” sentence appears, but the page repeatedly substitutes release and experiment narration for landing-page copy.

### Inconsistencies
- “MIT-0 · Open Source” and the MIT-0 metadata description vs “Apache 2.0 License” in the footer.
- “No model fine-tuning required” vs a headline evidence card about a “Two-GPU parallel retrain”; the page never explains why retraining is relevant to a supposedly training-free product.
- HumanEval repair “+3.0 points” over 164 problems vs “66% → 84% (+18pp)” on HumanEval-50; the differing subsets and methods are not explained where the claims appear.
- Headline FoVer AUROC `0.9131` vs a former `0.9857` vs “0.90 AUC (vs 0.125 FoVer baseline)”; these may measure different things, but the labels are too vague for a stranger to tell.
- “Seven capabilities” includes code, maths, constraints, reasoning, research operations, APIs, and TTC/PREM, while the evidence introduces safety classification, hardware, training, constrained decoding, and extraction as though they were equally central product capabilities.
- The page claims it “works with any LLM,” but presents no cross-model compatibility evidence.

### Missing essentials
- A one-sentence purpose is present: Carnot checks an LLM answer for internal consistency and suggests repairs.
- Installation is present through `pip install carnot-ebm` and the quick-start example.
- A trustworthy license statement is missing because the two displayed licenses conflict; neither is linked to canonical license text.
- Credible support for the numbers is missing. Cards lack direct artifact links, sample sizes, uncertainty, model versions, evaluation dates, comparable baselines, and failure cases.
- “Checked-in artifact” and a recomputation in a “non-operator environment” are not meaningful independent validation.
- A clearly identified maintainer is missing. “© 2026 Ian Blenke” does not state maintainer role, team, governance, or contact route.
- Scope boundaries are missing. The page does not clearly say which claims Carnot can verify, which require external tools, and which factual claims it cannot establish.
- Operational requirements are vague: the page alternates between a simple Python install, single-GPU examples, JAX, Rust, formal solvers, and specialized FPGA hardware without separating required from optional components.

### Fabrication signals
- “GSM8K extraction TP rate: 0.5 → 1.0” — a perfect rate with no sample count, confidence interval, or held-out protocol.
- “k=5 ensemble catches 60/60 attacks” — perfect performance on an apparently small, possibly constructed attack set.
- “2.0× speedup, identical losses” — exact scaling and exact equivalence without tolerances or repeated-run evidence.
- “0.0pp accuracy delta with 4.4% cost savings” — zero degradation stated more precisely than the visible methodology supports.
- “99.3% of wrong code flagged” — near-perfect detection without the denominator of wrong programs or false-positive rate.
- “Zero false positives” in “Carnot Dogfooding by the Numbers” — a perfect operational result without an independent labeling protocol.
- “0.90 AUC vs 0.125 FoVer baseline” — an AUC dramatically below random should trigger an explanation of label orientation or baseline failure.
- `0.9131` reported to four decimal places from a five-seed result — precision theater unless the confidence interval is shown beside it.
- Several meters are filled to 100% for incomparable claims such as “live on silicon” and “2.0× speedup” — the graphics imply perfect scores where no common scale exists.
- The blog advertises fabricated artifacts, fatal flaws, retractions, and cheating. Transparency can build trust, but concentrating these stories on the landing page makes the project itself look uncontrolled.

## WHAT'S WORKING
- The hero gives a concrete, plain-language description and an immediately visible installation command.
- “Extract → Check → Repair” and the `47 + 28` example provide an understandable mental model before the page descends into jargon.

## RECOMMENDED OPERATOR ACTIONS
1. Resolve the MIT-0/Apache-2.0 contradiction and link the canonical license.
2. Replace experiment, milestone, and test counts with at most three user-relevant outcomes.
3. Reduce the evidence grid to 4–6 primary benchmarks with direct artifact links, sample sizes, models, baselines, seeds, uncertainty, and dates.
4. Reconcile or explicitly scope the FoVer and HumanEval numbers so they cannot look contradictory or cherry-picked.
5. Remove internal release language such as “paper-v6,” “repinned,” and “operator-initiated upload.”
6. Move research operations, autonomous-agent plumbing, retraining, FPGA work, and TTC/PREM off the primary capabilities path unless they directly affect users.
7. Expand or remove every unexplained acronym and internal type name.
8. Qualify perfect and near-perfect claims, especially `1.0`, `60/60`, `0.0pp`, “identical,” and “zero false positives.”
9. Replace the incomparable percentage meters with honest numeric summaries or a small benchmark table.
10. Identify the maintainer or organization, provide a contact route, and state the project’s support/governance status.
11. Add a blunt limitations statement describing what Carnot can and cannot verify.
12. Reduce the blog block to three trust-building posts and move the failure-retrospective archive behind “See all posts.”
13. Correct the unmatched closing elements and put the TTC/PREM card inside the intended grid before publishing.
